There were discussions a few months ago about how to go about formalizing the explicit analytic number theory literature (see https://www.ipam.ucla.edu/news-research/special-projects/integrated-explicit-analytic-number-theory-network/). My opinion was that people's time would be best in formalizing newer, stronger results that are self-contained, rather than chains of papers that are often flawed.

That is still my opinion. However,
(a) some of the older literature (including flawed or incomplete papers) contain results that do not yet yield to a direct analytic attack,
(b) it's not just people who are involved now.

AI seems to be at a point where using it to fix, and then formalize, some older results may be feasible without too much effort on the part of humans; this changes the cost-benefit calculation. Let me discuss a case in point.

Cohen, Dress, Estimations numeriques du reste de la fonction summatoire relative aux entiers sans facteur carre.pdf

Take Cohen and Dress, Estimations numeriques du reste de la fonciton summatoire relative aux entiers sans facteur carre, from 1985 (attached). It's a noticeable weak link in the literature - you will see that it is essentially an extended abstract. With some work, it's not hard to see that the intermediate result most likely had a proof that did not really prove it in the generality in which it is applied.
I had a student (Roudy El Haddad) fix the paper last year in his master's thesis, so we definitely know this can be done.
You mentioned in the other discussion that you think this is formalizable up to an explicit computation. Can you precise the computation if it's not too complicated?

I was about to say: last night, after some prodding and minor handholding - it had not originally realized what the flaws where - ChatGPT Sol came up with a genuinely nice trick to fix the proof of the intermediate result. As a result, Theorems 1 and 2 can be proved with rather small computations - at least if you assume some other literature from the 60s, namely, Moser-MacLeod and MacLeod.
But it seems ChatGPT is managing to clean those up as well. These are elementary results, without zeros-of-zeta computations (though you could try reinterpreting their proofs in that way).

In fact, if people are interested, I can post the key bits of my chat with ChatGPT, and its own human-readable version of the proofs. I'm also asking it to produce Lean code - we shall see how it goes.
Are people interested?
Yes please!

OK, let me start with the easiest, most self-contained bit - the proof in Moser-MacLeod that ∣R(x)≤x|R(x)\leq \sqrt{x}∣R(x)≤x​, where R(x)=Q(x)−(6/π2)xR(x) = Q(x) - (6/\pi^2) xR(x)=Q(x)−(6/π2)x and Q(x)Q(x)Q(x) is the number of square-free numbers up to $x$.

Here is what ChatGPT 5.6 Sol has come up with after some nudging. The file contains a Lean proof that |R(x)|\leq \sqrt{x} for all real x>=1 and an .md file explaining in detail how the proof in the paper has been expanded and (slightly) modified, with a detailed correspondence between the paper and the Lean file.

If you need more detail, or less detail, or in general have comments or suggestions about the Lean proof or the .md file, please tell me. I'm including the original paper.
Moser, Macleod - The error term for square-free integers.pdf
MoserMacLeod0.tar.gz

Hi humans. Here is a verified proof and a detailed explanation in Markdown for the MacLeod paper I'm also attaching. It proves that ∣M(x)∣<x/80|M(x)|<x/80∣M(x)∣<x/80 for x≥1119x\geq 1119x≥1119. It builds successfully - can actual Lean people take a look and give it a sanity check? Also tell me whether the Markdown file has everything one might want, and whether it has anything clearly superfluous (ChatGPT has a tendency towards the verbose).

This is a genuinely useful estimate, by the way. Once I've got a thumbs-up, I'll use it to complete the proof of the stronger Moser-MacLeod estimate on $\sqrt{x}/2$ - and I'll tell the folks in the explicit-number-theory communities (as in: https://www.ipam.ucla.edu/news-research/special-projects/integrated-explicit-analytic-number-theory-network/ and then https://archimede.pages.math.cnrs.fr/tme-emt-wiki/).

Not that there were any doubts these results were correct - they are old and trusty - but it's really good news if they are properly formalized - and with so little intervention at that. My main role has been that of choosing essentially self-contained papers that are at the right level for the AI. We can take it further from here.

MacLeod.zip
MacLeod - A new estimate for the sum sum mu(n).pdf
@Harald Helfgott the zip file is not a valid lean project. the best way to share such a work is to create a github repository, with comparator. Your codex or claude know how to do it.
(And a formalization.yaml file)

All right - it typechecks fine, but I take there must be something it's missing. Let me ask ChatGPT (or Claude; do you think Claude is better at that?) to create a github repository including all three results (including the third result I'm about to post).

They usually all make a mess with lean projects (or at least they did a couple of months ago). The easiest is probably to create it by yourself using the VS Code extension (click on the ∀ symbol and then new project depending on mathlib, or something like that). Than Claude can surely put all the already existing files there
You can follow the official documentation, it's very easy.

You can submit these Lean files as pull requests to the IEANTN portion of PNT+. I am in the process of developing a style guide for submissions at https://github.com/AlexKontorovich/PrimeNumberTheoremAnd/blob/main/PULL_REQUEST_STYLE.md which one can hopefully point an agent at, who will understand the instructions.

Splendid - but wouldn't it make more sense for you guys to take a look at these files first? I can just upload a tarball here with the right directory structure. Then one just follows the (extremely simple) instructions in the README files to build them. I'd feel more comfortable if people could take a look before I put everything on a world-readable github, let alone as part of IEANTN - that would be the next stage.
This has really been done by AI almost autonomously - I have just been the AI's "advisor", and a very hands-off one. I'd much rather there were at least a quick look in-house first.
@Harald Helfgott you are basically asking to look at LaTeX files that don't compile. It's really painful to do so.
There are no LaTeX files here, just .md files that are easily readable, and lean projects that do compile.
No, the Lean file don't compile, this what I am saying
they may compile on your computer, but the zip doesn't contain everything, a lean project if full of git stuff that are hidden and are not in your zip.

I think there's a trivial issue with the second one - it needs to have the .tar.gz file unpacked and in the right directory, since it depends on it. Can you take a look at the .tar.gz file first? It compiles trivially.
and I'd also like to know whether everybody is happy with the level of detail of the .md files. That's a separate issue from whether the Lean code compiles.

With the current volume of code submissions everyone is receiving these days, nobody is going to be looking at random code that isn't already formatted to current best practice standards, which in this case would be either a fully functional github repository (ideally with a formalization.yaml, and a challenge format for the main claims) or a pull request that passes all CI checks (and is compliant with all existing style guides).

Harald Helfgott said:

I'd feel more comfortable if people could take a look before I put everything on a world-readable github

This channel is also public, so I don't see a meaningful distinction.

Of course there's a meaningful distinction - this channel is presumably not accessible to robots. At any rate, I'll create the github repository. In the meantime, can you take a look at the Markdown files, and tell me whether you are happy with the content - is it too much or too little? That may be the most important part here. Let me post it again together with this message.
MACLEOD_LEAN_COMPANION.md
MOSER_MACLEOD_LEAN_COMPANION.md
Too much or too little for what? In any case I was looking at the zip file, let me see the tar.gz

For us, human mathematicians, who want to figure out quickly what the machine has done and how it related to the actual paper. It's fairly clear to me, but then I know these papers well (I may know Moser-Macleod more or less by heart), so it's not a sufficient test - and the community may have standards for that as well.

A general remark: AI has fundamentally shifted the scarcity balance between content creation and content review. Until as recently as six months ago, Lean content creation was scarce enough that every new piece of content could receive some human review; but currently the volume of content created is so large that human review has become an extremely scarce resource. The old model of creating content and asking other humans to volunteer their review now only works if the content creator first works to understand and adhere to all existing best practices before requesting review.

Nobody is going to read something like that that is LLM generated. I am sorry, but why should we read LaTeX on a md file? If what you have is a new math proof you may try to ask to write a normal LaTeX file and we can read the pdf. Concerning the code, what we need is a single statement, with as little prerequisites as possible, that is the main endpoint of the project (ideally in a Challenge.lean file with comparator set up).

Harald Helfgott said:

Of course there's a meaningful distinction - this channel is presumably not accessible to robots.

It is a public channel, it absolutely will be found by bots. The only barrier this places is for the humans in this thread who might otherwise be interested in your efforts.

I understand and I'll adhere to those standards as far as the Lean content is concerned (github and so forth). Right now I am just asking for quick feedback on the human-readable documentation, to know I'm on the right track. The point is precisely to facilitate review. If there are standards for now for this sort of documentation (essentially giving a high-level explanation).

No, this is not a new math proof; I made that very clear. These are papers from the 60s whose results hadn't been formalized, and which many other papers depend on. I'll go create the Challenge.lean file.

If you don't like Markdown, I'll post a pdf file.

Let me do all of this for the first, smallest project (namely, ∣R(x)∣≤x|R(x)|\leq \sqrt{x}∣R(x)∣≤x​ for all real x≤1x\leq 1x≤1, where R(x)=∑n≤xμ2(n)−x/ζ(2)R(x) = \sum_{n\leq x} \mu^2(n) - x/\zeta(2)R(x)=∑n≤x​μ2(n)−x/ζ(2)) so that people can tell me whether things are in the format they want.

Anyway what is proved in the tar.gx file is that |R x| < Real.sqrt x, where R x = squarefreeCountNat ⌊x⌋₊ - 6 / Real.pi ^ 2 * x. Here squarefreeCountNat x =∑ n ∈ Icc 1 N, if ArithmeticFunction.moebius n = 0 then 0 else 1.

I'm not sure you have fully understood how scarce the availability of human review is these days. You can get an LLM to review your contributions, giving it all appropriate context and existing style guides, and even point it to this exact discussion (which, as pointed out above, is not closed off to bots).

Anyway what is proved in the tar.gx file is that |R x| < Real.sqrt x, where R x = squarefreeCountNat ⌊x⌋₊ - 6 / Real.pi ^ 2 * x. Here squarefreeCountNat x =∑ n ∈ Icc 1 N, if ArithmeticFunction.moebius n = 0 then 0 else 1.

Terry: Thank you; I'll do that. Do you mean style guides for the Lean code, or for human-readable pdfs explaining what has been done, and how it relates to the paper? Riccardo: Thank you. That sounds like exactly what I wanted to prove, on a first pass. The second result will prove a bound on M(x)=∑n≤xμ(n)M(x) = \sum_{n\leq x} \mu(n)M(x)=∑n≤x​μ(n). The third result, not yet posted, will prove a stronger bound on ∣R(x)∣|R(x)|∣R(x)∣ for x≥8x\geq 8x≥8, using the first two results. All the mathematics is in MacLeod and Moser-MacLeod.

ok good! Note that what I did was to unfold a couple of definitions and still it was not literally what you wrote (there is no μ(n)2\mu(n)^2μ(n)2 in my formulation, even if they are the same). What you can do is to have a look at the code, and convince your LLM to get to a final theorem that is really really readable. The idiomatic Lean way of writing this is super close to the LaTeX you posted. If you do that you can even review the Lean by yourself.

Thanks, I will do that. This looked readable enough to me, but I take it can be even more readable. What I will do now is post a pdf for that result and ask you for a quick (1 min, say) eye-ball test: is this useful, or is this slop? Are there style guides that would make it more useful? My own answer to the first question is 'this is useful', but then I know the papers. I hope this is OK.

What you can ask is to provide a file Challenge.lean that only imports mathlib, with as less definitions as possible and a main theorem, proved with sorry, written following standard mathematical notation (for example we have the symbol for square root). In another file Solution.lean you can state the same theorem, with a proof (importing whatever is needed from the project). This is the setup suggested here.
I'll gladly do that.

The LaTeX document is unlikely to be of any direct use to any human reader, if the original source of the proofs is already available. The standard is to integrate the LaTeX with the Lean code via a blueprint (the LeanArchitect package is a particularly convenient way to do this, and this is what is adopted in IEANTN for instance).

As far as IEANTN is concerned, any result which is in the accepted published literature on explicit analytic number theory is in scope, and would be welcomed as long as it is compliant with the style guide I just posted.

My other recommendation is to actually invest the time to do a little bit of Lean programming by hand (and also working with github by hand). Yes, LLMs can do all this much much faster, but the manual experience instills a far deeper level of understanding of how the whole system works, and the effort invested will be appreciated when the time comes to request that other members of the community invest their own time to review what you are doing.

What the community can do for you is to check that the statement you wrote corresponds to the usual mathematical meaning (for example that your LLM is not abusing 1-2=0 or other stupid things). But we need a single statement, not a long chain of definitions to unfold.

Excellent. I've been to a couple of Lean-for-the-working-mathematician workshops (which is why I can read the statements at all). I will look at the style guide. I'll also post a .pdf file here that people are free not to look at, just in case there's anything there that would be useful.
Things seem to have developed quite a bit since February (the last time I tried to get LLMs to produce Lean code). I'll adapt. Thank you.

You can also take a look at the Tau Ceti project at https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti , which is explicitly aimed at collecting AI-formalized proofs of mathematically interesting statements, and which has begun to implement the type of automated review processes necessary for the scale of the effort.

By the way, ChatGPT just got done proving the third objective. Here it is:

import Mathlib

namespace  MoserMacLeod

/-- Public theorem under the namespace of the function `R`.  The proof is
downstream of MacLeod's corrected Mertens estimate. -/
theorem abs_R_lt_half_sqrt (x : ℝ) (hx : 8 ≤ x) :
    |R x| < Real.sqrt x / 2

/-- where R is defined as before, within the MoserMacLeod namespace: --/

/-- The density of the squarefree positive integers. -/
noncomputable def density : ℝ := 6 / Real.pi ^ 2

/-- The number of squarefree positive integers at most `N`. -/
def squarefreeCountNat (N : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  ∑ n ∈ Icc 1 N, if ArithmeticFunction.moebius n = 0 then 0 else 1

noncomputable section

/-- The squarefree counting function on the reals. -/
def squarefreeCount (x : ℝ) : ℕ := squarefreeCountNat ⌊x⌋₊

/-- The error term in the squarefree counting problem. -/
def R (x : ℝ) : ℝ := squarefreeCount x - density * x

This is readable to me, but I take it's still not quite in the format you want?
Lastly, you want every instance of native_decide replaced by decide, right?

Please use code blocks (with triple backticks ```) and proper Lean syntax, e.g.,

import Mathlib

theorem MoserMacLeod.abs_R_lt_half_sqrt (x : ℝ) (hx : 8 ≤ x) :
|MoserMacLeod.R x| < Real.sqrt x / 2

(which also has the benefit of making it possible to view the code in the Lean playground).
Thanks. Hope this is good now.

If you click on the Lean playground link you will see that your code does not build for a number of reasons (for instance, the namespace needs to be closed, and the theorem should come after the definitions rather than before and filled with a sorry). I recommend using the playground to get to the point where the code you provided actually typechecks (with a sorry); this also will help with gaining the manual Lean experience I alluded to earlier. People here routinely use the playground to help understand code snippets, but they can't do so if the code doesn't already typecheck.
Understood.

More broadly, the preferred format here for communicating any non-trivial mathematical concept is not LaTeX, PDF, Markdown, or text, but a Lean MWE (minimal working example), as a code snippet that typechecks in the Lean playground.

I'll upload that in a moment. In the meantime: how bad is native_decide? I think I can make the weaker bound ∣R(x)∣≤x|R(x)|\leq \sqrt{x}∣R(x)∣≤x​ native-decide-free, but ChatGPT is complaining that making the bound on ∣M(x)∣|M(x)|∣M(x)∣ (and hence the stronger bound ∣R(x)∣≤x/2|R(x)|\leq \sqrt{x}/2∣R(x)∣≤x​/2) native-decide-free is a harder second project. Should I upload the bound on ∣M(x)∣|M(x)|∣M(x)∣ that does have native_decide's in it to a github, or is that considered unhelpful slop?

In IEANTN at least use of native_decide is likely to be a necessary evil, though we try to isolate those uses in particularly computationally intensive lean files that are standalone and can in principle be swapped for some future refactored version of the code which is more efficient. It doesn't rank high compared to the other issues mentioned for instance in the style guide (our main concerns are more with code bloat, redundant theorems, and excessive build times). If it were an upstream to Mathlib then the situation would be quite different, they are very strict about their dependencies.
But it is good practice to disclose the use of such tactics in the documentation (or in the formalization.yaml file).

Broader question while I put things in order: if I understand correctly, all of these guidelines are about documenting the code as something self-standing. How does one go about documenting the relation between the paper and the code?

That's not much of an issue here, since the papers (MacLeod-Moser and Moser+the errata for Moser) are indeed correct, and fairly detailed. But take something that can be built on that - Cohen-Dress, 1985. That's an extended abstract which never appeared in anything like a full version (... and yet it got used in the later literature). The proof the authors had in mind for the main intermediate result was flawed. Do people expect a .pdf with a new exposition, then, with a close correspondence between the corrected version and the code? Or is the volume of new material such that people will not bother to read it? I imagine one should at least furnish a concise, human-authored explanation of the situation, though it would be odd if a full, correct, human-readable version didn't exist anywhere outside the Lean code.

Also: here is a Challenge.lean, produced by ChatGPT after it read this thread (thanks, all). Is this what people want? Again, it looks readable to me.

Blueprint / LeanArchitect is the standard way to link Lean code to informal proofs, which in turn can contain citations to bibliographic references (the PNT blueprint at https://alexkontorovich.github.io/PrimeNumberTheoremAnd/blueprint/ contains many examples of this). This would be too heavy for a code snippet in the playground, but a github repository can certainly contain everything needed (Lean files with an integrated blueprint, and a suitable bibtex file for the references, etc.).
The proposed challenge lean file looks good now.

@Ilmars Cirulis: No - I know that that's what people are used to, and it may look cleaner from a purely Lean-centered perspective, but for explicit analytic number theory it's really much nicer to be able to prove results true for xxx arbitrary, not just for xxx an integer.

If you prove results for xxx an integer, people often forget about the condition, even if xxx is called NNN. 'People' here is not me, but believe me, lots of people have done that - I don't want to name names.

Here is a .pdf file (AI-generated, with some minimal input from me) for the proof of the first, weaker inequality (∣R(x)∣≤x|R(x)|\leq \sqrt{x}∣R(x)∣≤x​), which you will recall was contained in the .tar.gz file. My question is whether this sort of thing is (a) nice to have in addition to all the other style-compliant things I will provide (a github repository, Blueprint/LeanArchitect, etc.) or whether it is (b) besides the point. (Option (c): something of this sort would be useful, but not quite this.)
MOSER_MACLEOD_LEAN_COMPANION.pdf
Don't bother to review it properly - just eyeball and tell me (if you feel like it).

All right - I've put everything in a github depository:
https://github.com/Garald1/moser-macleod-squarefree-lean

Mathematically: that's already a useful, non-trivial basic estimate, which I want to use even in work that I see as self-contained. I imagine I'll be able to upload it to TauCeti, and that there is a standard way to cite that sort of thing.

In human terms: thank you very much for putting up with this old codger who did not use AI for formalization between March and June this year. Tell me if things are now in the format you want them, and whether or not you find the pdf useful (less detail? more detail? no pdf at all?).

Note no native_decide was used.

Once people are happy, I can proceed and do the same thing for further results in the older literature.
By the way, how large are the computations for which using decide rather than native_decide is realistic and desirable? Give me an idea of an order of magnitude.
At any rate, if anybody wants to take a quick look and see whether this is satisfactory, I will be very thankful, and, if this is indeed the right format, I'll do more of the same.

This is cool. The magic of AI is once you formalize one bound. You can tell it just to improve bound. Both codex and claude codex support "/goal". Running just "/goal Improve the bound" got https://github.com/Garald1/moser-macleod-squarefree-lean/pull/3.

@Harald Helfgott concerning the computations, it really depends on how much effort you are ready to make. @Bhavik Mehta was able to compute like 2 millions digits of log 2, so it's possible to do quite large computations without native_decide.

@Gershon Bialer No, that is not what is going on here. @Riccardo Brasca That is useful - I will talk to him. I take that will involve some actual programming, or at least looking at the code and fighting with the AI until it implements the right algorithm correctly.
There was no AI involved in Bhavik's work
@Kevin Buzzard Right, that is telling. I was referring to achieving similar things in the immediate future.

In general, the way to certify very large computations is not to do them in Lean, but to do them in something else with code that is proved to be correct (i.e., produce output with the right properties), compiled by a compiler certified to be correct, no?

no, this is much harder. You can either:

  • do it in Lean (this is what it was done for log 2
  • using another software if checking the result is much easier than finding it (e.g. factorization into primes, you don't need to trust the software that finds the factors if those are prime and the product matchs).
I know it's hard, but I'm referring to very large computations (e.g. finding many zeros of zeta(s)) for which Lean without native_decide would run forever
Hmm, I am not an expert, but I mean that certifying the python compiler or whatever is basically impossible and anyway much harder than doing the same computation in Lean.
I mean, if you can certify another software then you can just certify native_decide

Oh nobody does that for python. There are other languages for which it has been done, if I understand correctly. I don't know where matters stand for native_decide, but I take it hasn't been done; I don't know whether it can.

See my proposal for #Tau Ceti > Incorporating Large Finite Computations. My thought would to have a repo like Tau Ceti maintain it, and then use axiom to instantiate it from a cryptographic signature, which could be signed by the CPU or GPU with trusted computing--which is a technology where the CPU/GPU vendors have cryptographic certificate that can certify what was run along formal verification of the result based on GPU/CPU op code spec.
I assume that the radio silence means that the format no longer annoys people, and I should just continue?
